newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK to sing--Who wants to be a (paper) millionaire?.
newsitem.headline: HK to sing--Who wants to be a (paper) millionaire?.

text.p: Money-crazed collectors can become paper-millionaires soon with a Hong Kong 97' $1 million souvenir banknote to mark the British colony's return to Chinese rule.

But don't try spending it. The special currency issue, printed on Bank of England presses, can't be exchanged for cash, almost like the predicament actor Gregory Peck faced in the 1953 movie, "The Million Pound Note."
In that comedy, from a story by American writer Mark Twain, a man is given a million pounds in the form of a single banknote and finds it difficult to spend.
Money World Asia, exhibition organisers and currency distributors, said: "It's a souvenir but looks real, using banknote technology, paper and presses."
Chua Mia Tee, a renowned currency designer who has painted well known personalities in Asia, created this commemorative note for the June 30 handover.
It features a portrait of Chinese patriarch Deng Xiaoping, the chief architect of China's economic reform, who died this year.
Deng, who had wanted to survive to see the handover, is seen smiling at the skyscraper backdrop of Hong Kong's famed Victoria Harbour of Hong Kong.
The note carries the mottos, "Return to The MotherLand, Joy to the World" and "One country two systems, Hong Kong people rule Hong Kong."
Money World Asia said the note were printed by the Bank of England's own 'Debden Security Printing using genuine currency paper with latest currency features incorporated.
So they are genuine except they're not legal tender. How much? Each souvenir note, with its own serial number, will be sold at HK$100 (US$13).
